roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So then why is there a burden?  I'm so confused.  I'm trying to understand what you mean, the litigation burden.  You -- you -- you also seem to say these are easily disposed of, that you want to  channel them into the veterans' scheme precisely because you can get a higher-up to come and say, oh, this was a rogue -- a -- a -- a Board of Veterans' Appeals person who thought it might be unconstitutional, but we're going to squelch that.  So what is the litigation burden?

Having to defend against meritless claims is still a great burden on the agency, particularly if  --if they have to do it all around the country from district courts and then up to all the regional courts of appeals.  A point I wanted to just tie off that I was going to make earlier was that Section 7292(c) goes out of its way to say the Federal Circuit shall have exclusive jurisdiction to decide challenges to the validity of statutes.  If Petitioner is correct, then that is essentially a nullity because anybody can go to  any district court around the country and then take that claim up to any court of appeals.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is that what they're doing now?
That's what --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, since this has been the prevailing system and you told Justice Kavanaugh that the problem for the government is the litigation burden of being all around the country, but given the government's position to this point, is that what's happening now?
Well, it hasn't been a huge deal yet because there are only two circuits, I think, that have adopted Petitioner's view.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It wasn't a problem up until last year when you took the opposite position in Pereida, right?
If -- if the Court --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's a real new problem.

-- if the Court were to adopt Petitioner's view and open the doors of  all the district courts around the country to these claims, we think it would be a serious problem because, again, as the Board decisions that we've cited in the briefs addressing these kinds of facial constitutional challenges show,  these claims are a lot more common than they were back in the '70s when Robison was decided. So we don't think that that concern can be dismissed.  We're totally in policy land at this point.  We think that the statutory text  resolves this case completely.  These claims are --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: On that, Mr. Barber, I mean, I suggested before that if all I do is look at 511 alone, I think you have the better of the argument. But Mr. Chen was right to point out that 511 is kind of Version 2 of the statute, and Version 1 went his way.  And then you look at the differences.  I think that those  -- the differences in terminology, you know, point your way, no doubt.  But, on the other hand, a -- a -- a court that was -- a Congress that was really set on reversing the Robison rule, it seems  very strange that it would do that by virtue of making the changes in that sentence.

I respectfully disagree with that.  And I think a good example of this is the Traynor versus Turnage angle because  Petitioner accepts that one of Congress's purposes in enacting the VJRA was to abrogate this Court's decision in Traynor.  It also did that in a relatively subtle way.  It changed that second clause --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, subtle --
-- of the first sentence  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- but pretty darn clear.
Well, we  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I think that the first part of the sentence, you know, you  -- you -- you have to struggle a good deal more to understand how that changes the issue.

We think this is also pretty darn clear moving that "question of law" clause away from the "under any law affecting the provision of benefits" clause.  We think that's clear.  And that's just looking at  511(a) in isolation, which you would never do. You would also want to look at Chapter 72.  And  we think that that statutory context really eliminates any doubt.  Another case I would point you to is Weinberger.  It was decided the year after  Robison.  That case had an express preclusion clause referring to claims arising under Title II of the Social Security Act.  You said that  that clause applied to constitutional challenges to the Act even though it's pretty  unnatural to say that such a claim arises under the Act.  If that clause covered constitutional  claims, we don't see how this one couldn't.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If it goes to district courts, where does the appeal go?  Do all the appeals go to the Federal Circuit still?
No.  No, we don't think that would work that way at all, which is why the 7292(c) --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, that's  --
-- would be defeated.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- what do we do with  --this is, I guess, a helpful question for you.  That says exclusive jurisdiction.  So  what do we do with that?
It says exclusive jurisdiction in cases brought under this  section, I think.  And so what that means is that you can't go from the Veterans Court to any court of appeals besides the Federal Circuit.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mm-hmm.
But, by its terms, that provision would not prevent you, assuming you could file these claims in district court  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It says, "exclusive jurisdiction to decide any challenge to the validity of any statute or regulation." I guess you're saying brought under this section.  I was wondering, you know.
Yeah.  It's the "under this section" language that is problematic.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.  Got it. Thank you.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Let me go back to your exchange with  --with Justice Kagan.  I  -- I  -- I guess one might expect for Congress, if it was targeting Robison, to say all questions  of law and fact, including constitutional issues or something, given that this Court had said questions of law and fact under a law does  not include constitutional questions.  So can you say a little bit more about why you think that, looking at 511 after 211, the changes are enough to indicate Congress's  intent to move away from Robison?

Sure.  I mean, I think we have to look at the actual statutory text, not hypothetically hyper-clear statutory text.  We think that the statutory text is quite clear here, particularly in conjunction with Chapter 72, which  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How is -- how is 211 different than 511 in a way that matters?

I think the key difference in this case is separating -- so the "question of law" clause from the "under a law" clause.  The previous version of the statute said decisions of the administrator on any  question of law or fact under any law administered by the VA.  That was at least plausibly read, particularly in light of the Court's  constitutional concerns in Robison, as  referring to questions of law arising under the statute itself relating to its interpretation or application.  By saying "all questions of law and fact necessary to a decision by the Secretary," that naturally invites the inclusion of constitutional challenges to the statute because, as Justice Kagan was explaining, it's  obviously necessary to a decision under or in accordance with the statute if you define it that way to determine whether the statute is constitutional in the first place.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  I'm going to have to look because I'm looking at 211 that says, "the administrator shall decide all questions of law and fact necessary to a decision by the administrator under a law," which seems like it's the same --
That's the current version.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's the current version?  Okay.
Yeah.  That's not the Robison version.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  Got it. Thank you.
Yep. I don't have anything more to add, so we can proceed to seriatim.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  Justice Thomas?  Justice Alito? Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kagan?  I can't quite see you there.  Justice Barrett, anything further? Justice Kavanaugh, anything further? Thank you, counsel.
Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Rebuttal, Mr. Chen?

Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice.  So, on the distinction between attacks on statutes on one hand, which, in this context, has been called facial, versus attacks on agency action, that line is -- has proven to be quite  --lower courts have at least been able to  --have been able to draw that line perfectly adequately.  We have decades of experience from Robison, from 1974, where lower  courts have developed these simple tests to figure out whether a challenge is actually to a statute versus whether it's  --whether it attacks the inherent characteristics of a statute versus whether it attacks agency action.  And we also know that this is both before and after the VJRA was passed in 1988, because, after 1988, most lower courts have -- most lower courts have adhered to the line that Robison drew.  Not only that, the BVA has  continued to draw that line perfectly adequately.  They have to identify  -- they consistently identify what challenges they can and cannot decide.  So I want to talk about this idea of  -- so I want to address the government's other proposed solutions to this Article II problem.  The government says that the Secretary could order reconsideration of a BVA's -- the BVA's decisions.  That's not right.  The  --the Secretary can't do that.  The -- only the BVA  chairman can order reconsideration of a BVA proceeding.  But even if, even if the government was correct that the Secretary could order the BVA to keep on ordering  reconsiderations until the Secretary's outcome  -- preferred outcome was reached, that is the exact kind of back-channel jury-rigging that this court in Arthrex held was insufficient for purposes of the Appointments Clause.  So, even  -- even -- even granting the government all those things, it still doesn't work under the Appointments Clause.  I think the government also alluded to this sort of instruction power about how somehow the government, the Secretary could dictate the outcomes of individual BVA proceedings using its instruction powers retrospectively or  --I think that not even -- not even the VA has construed the instruction power that broadly because it is quite startling.  And the reason it's startling is because Congress was very detailed in setting out the BVA's procedures.  Congress made  -- directed that the BVA has to make the agency's final decisions on all 511(a) matters.  It  precluded the Secretary from appealing them. It said that only the BVA chairman can order reconsideration.  And there is no provision that establishes direct review by the Secretary of the BVA's decisions.  All of those provisions would be meaningless if the  -- the --if the Secretary could, whenever it wanted to, retrospectively  --retrospectively dictate the outcome of individual BVA proceedings.  And, in fact, the VA, in its own GC opinion from 1992, says that the instruction power is just a term of art that refers to guidance documents published for newly enacted  -- or guiding newly enacted legislation prior to the issuance of reg  --issuance of regulations.  And so not even the government  thinks that the instruction power is -- is as broad as they are saying right now.  I want to talk about the asymmetric review provision.  The bottom line is that any  problems  --any constitutional problem that arises out of the asymmetric review provision is so much more serious on the government's reading of the statute because only the  government's reading of the statute opens the category of unreviewable BVA decisions to include decisions about whether to disregard an Act of Congress.  And that is a particularly weighty and significant exercise of  -- of executive power.  And then one thing I'd like to address is the -- my -- my friend directed you to the case Weinberger, which did have -- did consider language about "claim arising under" the statute.  But what he didn't tell you is that Weinberger explicitly distinguished Robison and said that the language in Robison, the decision  --the "decision under the law" language in Robison was "quite different" from the "claim arising under" -- "under a statute"  language such that only the latter includes -- can include constitutional challenges to statutes.  I think that is all I have or want to address.  So I don't want to keep us from lunch and  --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  The case is submitted.
